content: Common bunt, also referred to as stinking smut or covered smut, is a disease that affects both spring and winter wheat. It is caused by two closely related fungal species: Tilletia tritici (synonym T. caries) and Tilletia laevis (synonym T. foetida). Symptoms Plants infected with common bunt may exhibit moderate stunting, but the disease is not easily identifiable until the plants approach maturity. Even at this stage, the symptoms are often subtle. Following infection, the entire wheat kernel is transformed into a structure called a sorus, which consists of a dark brown to black mass of fungal teliospores. This mass is encased in a thin, papery outer layer derived from the kernel's periderm. These sori, commonly referred to as bunt balls, are light to dark brown in color and resemble wheat kernels, though they are typically more spherical in shape. Infected wheat heads, known as bunted heads, are slender and have a bluish-green hue. These heads may remain green for a longer period compared to healthy wheat heads. As the bunt balls mature, they turn a dull gray-brown color and become more noticeable. At harvest, the fragile outer covering of the bunt balls ruptures, releasing large quantities of spores into the air, which often appear as clouds. These spores emit a distinct fishy odor. Intact sori may also be found mixed with harvested grain. Disease Cycle During harvest, millions of fungal spores are released, contaminating healthy wheat kernels, other plant parts, or the surrounding soil. These spores can persist on the surface of kernels or remain viable in the soil. The disease begins when teliospores, particularly those on seeds or in the soil, germinate in response to moisture. The germination process produces fungal hyphae, which infect germinating wheat seeds by penetrating the coleoptile (the protective sheath covering the emerging shoot) before the plants emerge from the soil. Cool soil temperatures, ranging from 5°C to 10°C, are conducive to infection. Once inside the plant, the fungal hyphae establish themselves in the apical meristem (the growing tip of the plant) and spread systemically throughout the plant. After the initial infection, the fungal hyphae remain sparse within the plant until the formation of the wheat spikes. At this stage, as the ovaries begin to develop, the fungus proliferates within the spikes. Sporulation occurs in the endosperm tissue, eventually converting the entire kernel into a sorus filled with teliospores, which are encased in the thin, papery periderm. Pathotypes Distinct pathogenic races of the common bunt fungi have been identified. These races exhibit a classic gene-for-gene interaction with their wheat hosts, meaning that specific fungal genes correspond to specific resistance genes in the host plant. Management Effective management of common bunt involves several strategies, including the use of clean, uncontaminated seed, chemical seed treatments, and the cultivation of resistant wheat varieties. Historically, seed treatments with organomercury fungicides were highly effective in controlling the disease, reducing its prevalence to manageable levels. Modern systemic seed treatment fungicides, such as carboxin, difenoconazole, and triadimenol, are also highly effective against common bunt. However, resistance to certain fungicides has been reported.
